reading.rtitle: Defending Your Position in a Hospital Meeting
paras: In a hospital, people debate decisions every day: budgets, schedules, new equipment and new protocols. Nurses often have the best information, but many of them stay quiet in meetings. Defending your position is not about winning. It is about helping the team make a better decision.

First, start with a clear claim in one sentence: 'I believe every new nurse needs forty hours of simulator training.' Then give your reasons. A compelling argument uses data, real cases and the experience of the team. An opinion without evidence is easy to ignore.

Second, show that you listened. Before your counterargument, accept the part of the other view that is valid. Use although, even though or while with a full sentence: 'Although the training is expensive, it reduces errors.' 'While I understand your concern about time, safety comes first.' With despite, use a noun or an -ing form, never a full sentence: 'Despite the cost, the training saves money in the long term.'

Third, be honest about the drawbacks. Every proposal has one, and people trust you more when you mention it first. Then explain why the benefits outweigh the costs. Finally, look for common ground. You will not always persuade everyone, but if you stand by your position calmly and with good reasons, people will listen to you next time.

listenings.text: Hi Andreia, it's Paul from Boston. Before Thursday's meeting, I want to explain my position, so there are no surprises. I think we should cut the simulator training for new nurses from forty hours to twenty. Although the simulator is a great tool, forty hours is a lot of time for nurses who are already very busy. Our budget is also smaller this year, and we need to save money somewhere. Despite that, I know this training is important to you and to your team. So I am open to a real debate. Please bring your data and your best arguments. If your argument is compelling, I am happy to change my mind. See you on Thursday.

Thank you, Paul. I understand your concern, and your point about the budget is valid. But I stand by my position: new nurses need forty hours on the simulator. Although the training takes time, it reduces errors in the operating room. Last year, the nurses with forty hours of practice were faster and more confident in real surgeries. Even though twenty hours looks cheaper, one mistake with a patient costs much more. So, despite the smaller budget, I believe the benefits outweigh the costs. Here is my proposal: forty hours for new nurses and twenty hours for experienced nurses. I think that is common ground for all of us.

extra_audio.text: Here is how Andreia defends her position in the meeting. First, she makes a clear claim: new nurses need forty hours of training. Then she accepts that Paul's point about the budget is valid. Next, she gives her counterargument with real data from last year. After that, she explains why the benefits outweigh the costs. Finally, she proposes some common ground for both teams.
